scope: Additional independent numerical and mark-point quality check for six original first-school-mock AQA AS Physics Waves questions, without making new flashcards or changing any existing prompt

entries.subject: Physics
entries.prompt: A stationary wave on a stretched string has vibrating length L = (0.750 ± 0.008) m, tension T = (18.0 ± 0.7) N and mass per unit length μ = (0.0080 ± 0.0002) kg m⁻¹. The fundamental frequency is f = (1/2L)√(T/μ). (a) Calculate f. (b) Predict f if the tension is quadrupled while L and μ stay fixed. (c) Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the original f by adding relevant maximum fractional uncertainties. (d) State the physical reason for keeping the mode number fixed when comparing frequencies. [7 marks]
entries.modelAnswer: Substitute in f = (1/2×0.750)√(18.0/0.0080). The fundamental frequency is f = 31.6 Hz (approximately). Four times the tension doubles f because f is proportional to √T. The new fundamental frequency is approximately 63.2 Hz. Percentage length uncertainty = 0.008/0.750 × 100 = 1.07%. Percentage uncertainty in f ≈ 1.07 + ½(0.7/18.0 × 100) + ½(0.0002/0.0080 × 100) = 4.26%. Different harmonics have different frequencies; compare the same fundamental mode so observed changes follow the tested variable.
markPoints: The fundamental frequency is f = 31.6 Hz (approximately).
Four times the tension doubles f because f is proportional to √T.
The new fundamental frequency is approximately 63.2 Hz.
Percentage length uncertainty = 0.008/0.750 × 100 = 1.07%.
Different harmonics have different frequencies; compare the same fundamental mode so observed changes follow the tested variable.

entries.subject: Physics
entries.prompt: In a Young double-slit data analysis, the distance across eight consecutive fringe intervals is (16.0 ± 0.5) mm. Slit separation a = (0.350 ± 0.010) mm and screen distance D = (1.40 ± 0.02) m. (a) Determine the mean fringe width w. (b) Use w = λD/a to calculate wavelength λ in metres and nanometres. (c) Estimate its maximum percentage uncertainty from the given readings. (d) Explain why several intervals were measured together. [7 marks]
entries.modelAnswer: Eight intervals across 16.0 mm give w = 16.0/8 = 2.00 mm. Convert w = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m and a = 3.50 × 10⁻⁴ m. Rearrange λ = wa/D. λ = 2.00×10⁻³ × 3.50×10⁻⁴ / 1.40 = 5.00×10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. Percentage uncertainty from fringe span = 0.5/16.0 × 100 = 3.13%. Maximum percentage uncertainty in λ ≈ 3.13 + (0.010/0.350×100) + (0.02/1.40×100) = 7.41%. Measuring several fringe intervals together reduces the percentage reading uncertainty compared with measuring one tiny gap.
markPoints: Eight intervals across 16.0 mm give w = 16.0/8 = 2.00 mm.
Convert w = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m and a = 3.50 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Rearrange λ = wa/D.
Percentage uncertainty from fringe span = 0.5/16.0 × 100 = 3.13%.
Maximum percentage uncertainty in λ ≈ 3.13 + (0.010/0.350×100) + (0.02/1.40×100) = 7.41%.
Measuring several fringe intervals together reduces the percentage reading uncertainty compared with measuring one tiny gap.

entries.subject: Physics
entries.prompt: A string has vibrating length L=0.800 m and mass per unit length μ=0.640 g m⁻¹. (a) Convert μ to SI units. (b) Calculate the first-harmonic frequency at tension T=16.0 N using f=(1/2L)√(T/μ). (c) Explain why f² against T is a straight line and calculate the theoretical gradient. (d) State the factor by which f changes if T rises from 16.0 N to 36.0 N. [7 marks]
entries.modelAnswer: μ=0.640/1000=0.000640 kg m⁻¹. f=(1/(2×0.800))√(16.0/0.000640)=98.82 Hz, or 98.8 Hz to three significant figures. Squaring yields f²=T/(4L²μ), so plotting f² vertically against T horizontally gives a straight line through zero with gradient 1/(4×0.800²×0.000640)=610.35 Hz² N⁻¹≈610 Hz² N⁻¹. If tension rises 16.0 to 36.0 N, frequency multiplies by √(36/16)=1.50, becoming about 148 Hz.
markPoints: Converts μ=0.640 g m⁻¹ to 6.40×10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹.
Uses f=(1/(2L))√(T/μ) with consistent SI units.
Calculates f≈98.8 Hz for T=16.0 N.
Squares to obtain f²=T/(4L²μ), predicting a straight line through the origin.
Gives gradient 1/(4L²μ) for an f²-versus-T graph.
Calculates gradient ≈610 Hz² N⁻¹ (610.35 to additional figures).
Uses f∝√T to find ratio √(36.0/16.0)=1.50 (revised f≈148 Hz is also acceptable).

entries.subject: Physics
entries.prompt: A plane transmission grating has 600 lines per mm. Monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm is incident normally. (a) Determine the slit spacing, the angle of the second-order maximum, and the greatest possible whole order. (b) Explain how changing to longer-wavelength light affects the angle of a given non-zero grating order. (c) For a separate single slit, explain how narrowing the slit or increasing the wavelength affects the angular width of the central maximum. (d) Two in-phase coherent sound sources produce loud and quiet regions. State what makes them coherent and explain the path-difference conditions for a loud and a quiet region. [10 marks]
entries.modelAnswer: A grating with 600 lines per mm has slit spacing d = 1/(600000) = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m. For the second order, sin θ = 2λ/d = (2 × 500 × 10⁻⁹)/(1.67 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 0.600. The second-order diffraction angle is θ ≈ 36.9° to the normal. The greatest possible whole diffraction order is 3 because m ≤ d/λ ≈ 3.33. For a fixed grating and order, increasing wavelength increases sin θ and therefore the diffraction angle. Reducing the width of a single slit makes its central diffraction maximum wider. Using a longer wavelength with the same single slit also makes the central maximum wider. Two sound sources must have the same frequency and constant phase difference to remain coherent. A loud sound region can arise where waves reinforce, at an integer-wavelength path difference for sources in phase. A quiet sound region can arise where waves cancel, at an odd-half-wavelength path difference for sources in phase.
markPoints: A grating with 600 lines per mm has slit spacing d = 1/(600000) = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m.
For the second order, sin θ = 2λ/d = (2 × 500 × 10⁻⁹)/(1.67 × 10⁻⁶) ≈ 0.600.
The second-order diffraction angle is θ ≈ 36.9° to the normal.
The greatest possible whole diffraction order is 3 because m ≤ d/λ ≈ 3.33.
For a fixed grating and order, increasing wavelength increases sin θ and therefore the diffraction angle.
Reducing the width of a single slit makes its central diffraction maximum wider.
Using a longer wavelength with the same single slit also makes the central maximum wider.
Two sound sources must have the same frequency and constant phase difference to remain coherent.
A loud sound region can arise where waves reinforce, at an integer-wavelength path difference for sources in phase.
A quiet sound region can arise where waves cancel, at an odd-half-wavelength path difference for sources in phase.

entries.subject: Physics
entries.prompt: A sinusoidal progressive wave moves in the positive x-direction at 60.0 m s⁻¹ and has frequency 125 Hz. At the same instant, two points 0.090 m apart on the wave have different phases. (a) Calculate the period and wavelength. (b) Find the fraction of a cycle and phase difference in degrees and radians between the two points. (c) Find the equivalent time delay and state which point lags, if the point further along +x is the second point. [7 marks]
entries.modelAnswer: Period T = 1/f = 1/125 = 0.00800 s. Wavelength λ = v/f = 60.0/125 = 0.480 m. Spatial separation as fraction of a cycle is 0.090/0.480 = 0.1875 cycles. Phase difference = 0.1875 × 360° = 67.5°. Phase difference in radians = 0.1875 × 2π = 1.18 rad. Equivalent time delay is 0.1875 × 0.00800 = 0.00150 s = 1.50 ms. For a wave moving +x, the downstream point lags the upstream point by 67.5°.
markPoints: Wavelength λ = v/f = 60.0/125 = 0.480 m.
Spatial separation as fraction of a cycle is 0.090/0.480 = 0.1875 cycles.
Phase difference = 0.1875 × 360° = 67.5°.
Phase difference in radians = 0.1875 × 2π = 1.18 rad.
Equivalent time delay is 0.1875 × 0.00800 = 0.00150 s = 1.50 ms.
For a wave moving +x, the downstream point lags the upstream point by 67.5°.

entries.subject: Physics
entries.prompt: Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of frequency 680 Hz in air where the sound speed is 340 m s⁻¹. At observation point A, the sound has travelled distances 4.00 m and 4.75 m from the speakers. The waves were emitted in phase. At observation point B, the distances are 4.00 m and 5.00 m. (a) Find the wavelength and the path difference at A in wavelengths. (b) Predict constructive or destructive interference at A and at B. (c) Explain the significance of coherence and why complete silence at A is not guaranteed. [7 marks]
entries.modelAnswer: Sound wavelength λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.500 m. Path difference at A is 4.75 − 4.00 = 0.750 m. At A, path difference is 0.750/0.500 = 1.50 wavelengths. A is a destructive-interference position because path difference is an odd half-wavelength for in-phase sources. At B, path difference is 5.00 − 4.00 = 1.00 m = 2.00 wavelengths, giving constructive interference. Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, maintaining a stable interference pattern. Complete cancellation at A requires equal wave amplitudes at that point; unequal amplitudes leave some resultant sound.
markPoints: Sound wavelength λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.500 m.
Path difference at A is 4.75 − 4.00 = 0.750 m.
At A, path difference is 0.750/0.500 = 1.50 wavelengths.
A is a destructive-interference position because path difference is an odd half-wavelength for in-phase sources.
At B, path difference is 5.00 − 4.00 = 1.00 m = 2.00 wavelengths, giving constructive interference.
Coherent sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference, maintaining a stable interference pattern.
Complete cancellation at A requires equal wave amplitudes at that point; unequal amplitudes leave some resultant sound.
